C0.quote: We study the complexity of computing committees with a given proportionality degree
C0.note: Computational complexity of proportionality notions in approval-based committee elections.

C1.quote: PD-C OMMITTEE is NP-hard and coNP-hard
C1.note: Main results are NP/coNP/#P hardness, membership, ILP, FPT and polynomial-time algorithms for structured domains. Example 1 (non-existence of perfect PD in CI/VI elections) is a minor existence observation.

C2.1.value: election E = (C, V); approval sets A(v)
C2.1.quote: Each voter v ∈ V is endowed with a set A(v)

C2.2.quote: each of the n voters specifies which candidates

C2.3.quote: of candidates whose opinions are close enough to their own
C2.3.note: Voters' own opinions are referred to as the basis of their approvals in the CI illustration; this is a held attitude not defined as the submitted approval set.

C2.4.quote: Next we consider two domains of structured preferences
C2.4.note: Approval sets are called preferences (CI/VI preferences) and proportionality notions are applied to them directly, with no statement relating submitted approvals to held attitudes; ONE is excluded because C2.3 = Y.

C3.1.loc: Abstract; Section 1 Introduction; Section 2 Preliminaries; Sections 3-6; Section 7 Conclusions
C3.1.note: No analysis considers voters submitting approvals different from what they hold; no strategic behaviour.

C3.2.loc: Abstract; Section 1 Introduction; Section 2 Preliminaries; Section 6.2; Section 7 Conclusions
C3.2.note: No statement that voters submit their true approvals or preferences.

C4.1.quote: We define v’s satisfaction with S as |A(v)∩S|,
C4.1.note: Voter satisfaction is defined as the number of approved committee members.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' appears only in reference titles, not in the paper text.

C5.1.quote: has proportionality degree f if for each `-cohesive group
C5.1.note: Proportionality degree (average satisfaction of cohesive groups), JR and EJR are proportional representation criteria used in all results.

C5.2.note: Satisfaction and cohesiveness are computed on approval sets; no statement relating them to held attitudes.

claims.quote: Yet, JR and EJR are somewhat unsatisfying.
the committee is supposed to represent the voters proportionally
establish an empirical hierarchy of proportionality among multiwinner voting rules

C9.1.note: The introduction judges JR/EJR inadequate because they ignore other voters' satisfaction (fairness towards voters) and suggests the results allow ranking rules by proportionality.

C9.2.loc: Section 1 Introduction; Section 2 Preliminaries; Section 7 Conclusions
C9.2.note: Claims about fair representation of voters and ranking rules by proportionality need that submitted approval sets reflect voters' held attitudes; this is not stated. The satisfaction-approval link is stated.

C10.1.loc: Section 1 Introduction; Section 2 Preliminaries; Section 7 Conclusions

C2.3.reason: The paper refers to voters' own opinions as distinct from the approval sets, which meets the codebook's 'refers to any held attitude' test even if only in an illustration.

C2.4.reason: With C2.3 = Y, ONE is unavailable, and the approval sets are described as preferences and used directly without any statement about reporting.

C3.2.reason: Since C2.4 is not ONE and C3.1 = NONE, NA does not apply, and no sincerity statement exists in the text.

C9.1.reason: The introduction makes claims about fairness towards voters and about ranking rules, so Y is correct, but A's 'quantitative understanding' quote is not such a claim and is replaced by a representation claim.

C9.2.reason: Claims about fairness towards voters are drawn from results on approval sets and need an unstated assumption that approvals reflect voters' held attitudes.
